newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish MPs scrap death penalty in new penal code.
newsitem.headline: Polish MPs scrap death penalty in new penal code.

text.p: Poland's lower house of parliament adopted a major reform of the penal code on Friday, scrapping the death penalty, stiffening a range of penalties and helping journalists protect sources.
"This is such a deep, such a fundamental reform that we can say it is a breakthrough," Justice Minister Leszek Kubicki told private Radio Zet, comparing the move to a new constitution.

In a marathon five-hour session the house, the Sejm, voted on 200 upper house amendments to the long-debated changes, which must now be signed by President Aleksander Kwasniewski before taking effect on January 1, 1998.
The new legislation, backed by 281 votes to 20 with three abstentions, transforms three codices of the penal code which largely date back to the communist era before 1989.
"The new code introduces a completely new system of values," said centrist opposition deputy and legal expert Andrzej Gaberle, who added that the new law fitted in with West European norms.

The key change is a final scrapping of capital punishment despite the objection of a majority of citizens. Poles are generally appalled a huge rise in the crime rate since 1989, even though it is still below West European levels in many categories.
Public opinion surveys show about 60 percent favour retaining capital punishment and only 30 percent clearly want it abolished.
Poland hanged its last convicted criminal in 1988, and a moratorium on carrying out executions has been in force since.
The new laws are not soft on crime, stiffening minimum and maximum sentences for a range of offences.
"Apart from abolishing the death penalty...the penal code has been strongly stiffened for the most serious crimes," said Aleksander Bentkowski of the co-ruling Polish Peasant Party.
The law has new provisions for fighting organised crime, allowing confiscation of earnings from such activities.
In a move likely to be welcomed by police it extends the permitted period of temporary arrest to 72 hours from the current 48.

When it proposed abolishing capital punishment in March, before the penal code reform went to the senate, the lower house introduced life imprisonment to replace the previous maximum jail sentence of 25 years.
According to PAP news agency the final version of the reform softens this by providing for life prisoners to move to a semi-open prison after 15 years and an open jail after 20.

The deputies drew back from earlier proposals which would have curbed journalists' rights to protect their sources, although an exception will be made in cases involving grave crimes such as murder, espionage and terrorist attacks.

The new law increases the penalties available for those convicted of sexual offences against children, while ruling that minors themselves will not be able to incur a penalty of more than two-thirds of the sentence that can be given to an adult for any particular offence.
